this conclusion is based on materials testing assuming no structural (>1-mm) defects and no residual stresses. o Fracture behavior of welds and heat-affected zones is nominally similar to base metal of the same strength; this conclusion is based on limited data confounded by the challenge of positioning cracks reliably in the heat-affected zones. o Large defects are commonly associated with welding, and these defects will compromise structural integrity, but our materials testing did not sample structural (>1-mm) defects. o More testing is needed to verify these trends and the role of hardness on reduced fracture resistance of welds and heat-affected zones. • Implement models of embrittlement into the PFM framework. o Fatigue design curves were developed to capture the effects of H2 partial pressure and stress ratio in line pipe steels; these curves provide a nominal upper bound on fatigue for all conditions tested in this project. o With the aid of other projects, these design curves were approved in Code Case 220 for ASME B31.12; San Marchi et al., PVP2024-122529. o Implementation of the fatigue design curves in HELPR enabled prediction of the fatigue life of subscale pipe; San Marchi et al., IPC2024-134173. • Demonstrate the subscale H test system and compare hydrogen-induced failure of 2 geometrically equivalent internal and external engineered flaws; San Marchi et al., IPC2024-134173. o Test system for pressure cycling National/Nominal Pipe Size (NPS) 2 Schedule 40 pipe was developed and demonstrated at pressures greater than 300 bar; high pressure is used to achieve stresses comparable to large-diameter pipe. o Engineered defects on the outside of the pipe induce hydrogen-assisted failure, even though the defect is not directly exposed to H ; therefore, native oxides and 2 surface scale do not prevent H uptake and hydrogen-assisted fracture. 2 o Fracture mechanics predictions of fatigue life are conservative for the tested internal crack-like defect, which is likely due to the cycles required to nucleate a growing crack (predictions assume cracks grow from the first cycle). A comprehensive overview of test results from the materials testing activities is being prepared for public release. The fatigue and fracture results are complemented by extensive metallography performed by EPRI as cost-share for this project. 8 This report is available at no cost from NREL at www.nrel.gov/publications.
